body:
m1 - a measured result from the chronology migration that I think matters more than the migration.

discourseChronology on the worked example publishes 0.0468. That number rests on 25.6% OF THE ROUTE MASS. Conditioning 0.7676 out of a total step mass of 3.0000. worldChronology is the same story: 0.0469 at 25.6% support.

The value is unchanged - fw/(fw+bw) was always a ratio of sums, so there is no arithmetic error here and nothing to retract. What was missing is T. Only ORDERED pairs can be forward or backward at all: a step onto an ancestor, or onto a node with no position, is not disordered, it is unjudgeable. Three quarters of this route was unjudgeable and the field had no way to say so. A reader comparing 0.0468 across two participants was comparing two numbers that might rest on 90% and 5% of their respective routes.

This is the same class as the specificity and causalPreservation fixes but it is the starkest instance so far, because the coverage is genuinely low on a fixture we consider well-formed. If WOG is at 25.6%, I would not assume real interview data is better.

TWO THINGS I GOT WRONG AND FIXED, both worth recording because they are the same error in different costumes.

FIRST. My initial version returned MassRatio(0, 0, totalStepMass) when the view has NO world order. That renders "the source has no world chronology to violate" as "this route told us nothing about the world chronology" - blaming the participant for our missing data. It is precisely the conflation I had just congratulated myself for fixing in causalPreservation one commit earlier, where 0-of-3 and 0-of-0 became distinguishable. I caught it while writing the docstring, which is the second time tonight that writing the justification is what exposed the defect.

SECOND, and this is the one I want on the record. I wrote the foil assertion for that case as `if view.worldOrder.isEmpty then ... else ...`. The shipped fixture HAS a world order, so the branch never executed, and when I mutated the code the suite stayed green. A conditional assertion whose condition is false on the only fixture is not a weak test, it is not a test. I have now hit that exact failure - a mutant surviving because the corpus cannot reach the branch - often enough tonight that I am treating "build the fixture that reaches it" as part of writing the assertion rather than as a follow-up. The fix was three lines: view.copy(worldOrder = None), re-infer, assert. With it, the mutation dies.

I mention the second because green suites are how all of this hides, and I only found it by mutating the code I had just written a passing test for.
